meta.title: Did Louis XIV say "L'État, c'est moi"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Almost certainly not. The line is supposedly from the Parlement de Paris on 13 April 1655, but it appears in no register of that session. Its earliest printed appearance is 1818, in an essay by Pierre-Édouard Lémontey — 103 years after the king died.
meta.ogTitle: Did Louis XIV really say 'L'État, c'est moi'?
meta.ogDescription: No contemporary source records it. It surfaces in print in 1818, and on his deathbed the king said very nearly the opposite: 'I am going, but the State will always remain.'

answer.label: Almost certainly nobody said it — least of all in 1655
answer.sourceLine: The story is that a teenage Louis XIV strode into the Parlement de Paris on 13 April 1655 and silenced its objections with four syllables. The registers of that session do not contain them. No contemporary — not the memoirists, not the ambassadors, not the parlementaires who were in the room and had every reason to record an outrage — reports the king saying it. The phrase surfaces in print in 1818, in an essay by Pierre-Édouard Lémontey, and the nineteenth century did the rest.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None — absent from the parlement’s registers

trail: Start with the alleged occasion. In March 1655 Louis XIV held a lit de justice forcing through fiscal edicts, and the parlement kept debating them anyway; the king returned on 13 April to shut the discussion down. That confrontation is real. The sentence is not in the record of it the historical case ↗.

The trail then goes cold for a century and a half. Nineteenth-century French investigators looking for a source found that the attribution rested on tradition rather than testimony — there was simply no contemporary authority for the words a 19th-century inquiry ↗.

The earliest located printed instance is 1818, in Pierre-Édouard Lémontey’s essay on the establishment of the monarchy under Louis XIV, where he calls the four syllables the ‘Koran of France.’ Lémontey is now forgotten; his phrase is not.
source.excerptNote: Four syllables in French, which is part of why it stuck: l’état, c’est, moi. It is a brilliantly compact definition of absolutism — the sort of line a historian wishes a king had said, which is a good reason to check whether he did.
source.rightsNote: Both the phrase and Lémontey’s 1818 essay are long out of copyright everywhere, as is the Dangeau memoir recording the deathbed line. Reproduce them freely. Modern translations and scholarly editions of these texts are separate works with living owners. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Louis XIV
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Louis XIV
author.metaLine: 1638–1715 · King of France, the Sun King, reigned 72 years
author.bio: Louis XIV reigned for seventy-two years, built Versailles partly to keep the nobility where he could see them, and centralised French government to a degree no monarch before him had managed. If you needed one sentence to define absolute monarchy, he is the obvious mouth to put it in — which is exactly the problem. He wrote a great deal himself, including memoirs of instruction for his son, and the political theory in them is careful and dynastic rather than swaggering: the king is the servant of the state’s permanence, not its replacement.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the cleanest kind of apocryphal quotation: a scene everyone can picture, in a room whose minutes survive, saying something the minutes do not contain.

items.why: The 13 April 1655 session happened; the sentence is not in its registers, and no contemporary memoir, dispatch or pamphlet reports it. For a remark that would have been the political scandal of the season, that silence is decisive the record ↗.

Popular retellings have the sixteen-year-old king bursting in from the hunt in boots and whip to deliver the line. The costume detail attaches to the 1655 confrontation in later narratives, not to any contemporary account of him saying these words.

Lémontey put the four syllables into print in an essay on Louis XIV’s monarchy. Whether he coined them or repeated a salon commonplace is not settled — which is why we credit the quotation to nobody rather than to him.

items.scope: What he is recorded as saying
items.why: Dying in 1715, Louis XIV said « Je m’en vais, mais l’État demeurera toujours » — ‘I am going, but the State will always remain.’ That is the reverse claim: the state outlives the king. It is recorded in the memoir of the Marquis de Dangeau on the king’s death the attested line ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No contemporary source records it. The line enters print in 1818, and the king’s own attested last words say the state will outlast him — the opposite of the sentence he is famous for.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the shortest possible definition of a tyrant, which makes it irresistible to teachers, headline writers and anyone describing a leader who has confused himself with the office. Four syllables do the work of a chapter.

The irony is that Louis XIV’s actual project was the opposite of what the line describes. He spent seventy-two years building an administrative state durable enough to run without him — and then said so as he died.
detailsBody: 20 March 1655: Louis XIV holds a lit de justice forcing fiscal edicts through the Parlement de Paris.
13 April 1655: the king returns to stop the parlement debating them further. This session is real; the famous sentence is not in its registers.
1 September 1715: Louis XIV dies, having reportedly said ‘I am going, but the State will always remain’ — recorded by the Marquis de Dangeau.
1818: Pierre-Édouard Lémontey prints the four syllables and calls them the Koran of France.
The nineteenth century adopts the line as shorthand for absolutism, and it has never needed a source since.
context.pull: His attested last words say the state outlives the king. The famous line says the opposite.
